Arbiter is a simple publish/subscribe event system for communication between modules. All instances share the same subscribers, so a module can inform others without a reference to them. import Arbiter from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Arbiter'; const subscription = new Arbiter().subscribe('ORDER/READY', (order) => console.log(order)); // Somewhere else new Arbiter().inform('ORDER/READY', { orderId: 12300, total: 100.99, }); // When the callback is no longer needed, e.g. the component is removed subscription.remove(); Method Description subscribe(event, callback) Calls the callback with the arguments of every inform(). Returns a subscription, remove() removes it. unsubscribe(event, callback) Removes the callback. inform(event, ...args) Calls the subscribers of the event. informState(event, ...args) Like inform(), and callbacks subscribed later are called right away with these arguments. clearState(event) Forgets the arguments of informState(). clearSubscribers(event) Removes all subscribers of the event. getSubscribers(event) Returns the subscribers of the event. An error thrown by a subscriber doesn't stop the others. It's rethrown asynchronously, so it still shows in the console.

An event that happens once, like "the user is logged in", is easy to miss: a module that subscribes after it was informed would wait forever. Inform it with informState() instead, and later subscribers are called right away with the last arguments: new Arbiter().informState('USER/LOGGED_IN', user); // Later, e.g. in a module loaded afterwards new Arbiter().subscribe('USER/LOGGED_IN', (user) => greet(user)); // called right away Combined with ServerJS, the server can inform your modules too: OrderEvents.js import Arbiter from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Arbiter'; export default { ready(order) { new Arbiter().inform('ORDER/READY', order); }, }; $response->bigPipe()->require("require('OrderEvents').ready()", [$order]);

AsyncRequest sends a request to an endpoint that responds with the BigPipe response format. The DOM operations and modules of the response are applied automatically, before your handler is called. import AsyncRequest from 'bigpipe-util/dist/async/AsyncRequest'; const request = new AsyncRequest('/ajax/remove.php') .setMethod('POST') .setData({ id: 123 }) .setHandler((response) => { console.log(response.payload); }) .send(); // Cancel the request if it's no longer needed request.abort();

All setters return the request, so they can be chained. Method Description setURI(uri) The URL to call. It can also be passed to the constructor. setMethod(method) The HTTP method, POST by default. setData(data) An object (sent URL-encoded, nested objects as a[b]=c, null as an empty value, booleans as 1 and 0, undefined and empty arrays left out) or a FormData. setRequestHeader(name, value) Adds a request header. setRelative(element) The element that sent the request, see relative targets. setStatusElement(element) The element gets the status class while the request is running. setStatusClass(className) The status class, async-saving by default. send() Sends the request and returns the XMLHttpRequest. abort() Aborts the request. abandon() Aborts the request without calling its handlers, except the finally handler. setOption(name, value) Sets an option, see retries. setAllowCrossPageTransition(allow) Lets the request outlive its page, see below. Every request is sent with the X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest header and a __req parameter with a counter of the requests made from the page. A page transition abandons the requests of the page it leaves, so their responses never reach the next page. A request that must outlive its page, e.g. one that saves something in the background, calls setAllowCrossPageTransition(true).

Method Called setInitialHandler(fn) Right before the request is sent. setPreResponseHandler(fn) With the parsed response, before its DOM operations, pagelets and modules are applied. Returning false drops the response. setHandler(fn) With the parsed response, after its DOM operations and modules were applied. setErrorHandler(fn) With the XMLHttpRequest and the error when the request failed. setTransportErrorHandler(fn) Instead of the error handler, for failures without a BigPipe response: http, invalid_response, network and timeout errors. setFinallyHandler(fn) With the XMLHttpRequest after the request finished, successfully or not. setUploadProgressHandler(fn) With the upload ProgressEvent (loaded and total bytes) while the data is sent, e.g. a file. setTimeoutHandler(ms, fn) When there is no response in ms milliseconds: the request is aborted and fn gets a timeout error, or the transport error handler without fn.

When a response without an error has been handled, a success event bubbles from the relative element of the request, e.g. the link or form of the Primer, with the response as event.detail.response. For a streamed response it is dispatched with the last part. Listen to it on the element or any element above it: form.addEventListener('success', ({ detail }) => console.log(detail.response.payload));

The error handler gets the XMLHttpRequest and an error object, the same for every kind of failure: new AsyncRequest('/ajax/save') .setErrorHandler((xhr, error) => { if (error.isTransient) { // e.g. offer to try again } showMessage(error.summary, error.description); }) .send(); Property Description type Why the request failed, one of ERROR_TYPE exported by AsyncRequest, see below. code The code the server sent, or the HTTP status for http errors. status The HTTP status, 0 when there is no response. summary A short title of the error. description A sentence for the user. isWarning Always false: a warning is not an error, see below. isTransient Trying again may help: network errors, timeouts, 5xx and 429 statuses, or as the server marked it. payload The payload of a server error, null otherwise. server: the server sent an error with $response->setError(). The DOM operations and modules of the response are applied anyway, e.g. to mark an invalid field. An error the server marked as a warning ($isWarning) is not a failure: the handler gets the response, with its error, errorSummary and errorDescription. The response may have an error status, e.g. send(422): it is applied the same way, and status is the status. http: the server answered with a status other than 2xx, e.g. 404 or 500. Redirects are followed by the browser. A BigPipe response with an error status but without an error is applied too. invalid_response: the response is not a BigPipe response, e.g. a PHP fatal error page. network: there is no response, e.g. the browser is offline. timeout: there was no response in time, see setTimeoutHandler().

Requests without an error handler pass their errors to the default one, e.g. to show them in a dialog: import AsyncRequest from 'bigpipe-util/dist/async/AsyncRequest'; import Dialog from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Dialog'; AsyncRequest.setDefaultErrorHandler((xhr, error) => { new Dialog().showFromModel({ title: error.summary, body: error.description }); });

A token expires, e.g. with the session of the user, and the server then rejects the request. AsyncRequest gets a new token and sends the request again, once, so the user does not lose the form they filled in. The server can do it two ways: Answer with a new token. A response with "csrf_refresh": 1 that defines the CSRFToken module again says the request was rejected because of its token. The response is applied, which replaces the token, and the request is sent again with the new one. Its handlers are not called for the rejection; they are called for the second response. Name a refresh URL. When the CSRFToken module has a refresh URL and the server responds with 419 (the status Laravel uses for an expired token), the browser requests the URL, a response that defines the token, and then sends the request again. { "define": [["CSRFToken", {"token": "...", "header": "X-CSRF-TOKEN", "refresh": "/csrf-token"}]] } A request is sent again once: if the token is rejected again, the second response is handled like any other, or the 419 is an http error. If the refresh itself fails, the 419 is reported. A request that was abandoned meanwhile is not sent.

A request with the retries option is sent again right away when it fails with a network error, e.g. a dropped connection, as many times as the option says. The handlers are called once, for the last attempt. HTTP errors, invalid responses and timeouts are not retried. new AsyncRequest('/ajax/feed') .setMethod('GET') .setOption('retries', 2) .send(); Retry only requests that are safe to send twice, like GET requests: the server may have handled a request whose response was lost.

With the stream option, the request sends the __stream parameter, and the server can answer in parts, e.g. every pagelet as soon as it is rendered, see AsyncResponse::stream() in the PHP library. Every part is a response of its own: it is applied, and the pre-response handler and the handler (or the error handler) are called with it, as soon as it arrives. is_first and is_last of the response tell which part it is; the finally handler is called once, at the end. new AsyncRequest('/ajax/search') .setMethod('GET') .setOption('stream', true) .setHandler(response => { if (response.is_last) { spinner.hide(); } }) .send(); A server that doesn't stream sends a single response, with both is_first and is_last. A request whose response started arriving is not retried. The parts arrive over the same XMLHttpRequest, so CSRF tokens, timeouts and abandoning work as usual. See how it works for the format.

When the server defines the CSRFToken module, e.g. with BigPipe::setCSRFToken() in PHP, every request that can change data (not GET, HEAD or OPTIONS) sends the token, but only to URLs of the same origin: { "define": [["CSRFToken", {"token": "...", "header": "X-CSRF-TOKEN", "param": null}]] } header: the request header with the token, unless the request sets this header itself. param: the field of the data with the token. refresh: a same-origin URL that answers with a new token, see Token refresh. A later response that defines the module again replaces the token. Without the module, add the token yourself: const token = document.querySelector('meta[name=csrf-token]').getAttribute('content'); new AsyncRequest('/ajax/save') .setRequestHeader('X-CSRF-TOKEN', token) .send();

Bootloader loads the stylesheets and scripts of the page: the CSS and JS of the pagelets and of the modules the server calls. Every file is loaded once, also when two pagelets or two names point to it, and a <link rel="stylesheet"> or <script src> already on the page is not loaded again. With a Content Security Policy, the elements get the nonce of the page.

The server can name its files in a resource map, e.g. to send short names instead of long URLs with content hashes. A pagelet or a response carries the map in resource_map, and its css and js can then use the names: { "id": "feed", "css": ["feed.css"], "js": ["feed.js"], "resource_map": { "feed.css": {"type": "css", "src": "/static/feed.1a2b3c.css"}, "feed.js": {"type": "js", "src": "/static/feed.4d5e6f.js"} } } A name keeps the first resource it was given. Anything that is not a name in the map is a URL. A script that is an ES module, e.g. a chunk of Vite, has "module": true: it is added as <script type="module"> and preloaded with <link rel="modulepreload">. Its load event fires once it and its imports have run, so a module it registers is there when the callbacks run: { "resource_map": { "editor.js": {"type": "js", "src": "/build/assets/editor-4d5e6f.js", "module": true} } }

import Bootloader from 'bigpipe-util/dist/Bootloader'; Bootloader.setResourceMap({ 'editor.css': { type: 'css', src: '/static/editor.css' } }); Bootloader.loadResources(['editor.css', '/static/editor.js'], () => openEditor()); loadResources(names, callback, type) calls back once all the resources are loaded, right away when they already are. A script that fails to load is requested again twice, after half a second and after two more seconds. A resource that still fails counts as loaded, so one broken file does not stop the page: it is reported with an error and getErrorURLs() lists it, e.g. to load the page in full when a script is missing. A stylesheet that has not loaded after 5 seconds counts as loaded too, so a slow file does not hold up its pagelet and the JS of the page. A URL that is not in the map is loaded as the given type, or by its extension (.css as a stylesheet, anything else as a script). Scripts run in the order they were added.

A module that the page rarely needs, like an editor, does not have to be in the bundle of the page. The server lists the resources it needs in bootloadable, with a pagelet or a response, and ServerJS loads them before it calls the module: { "resource_map": { "editor.css": {"type": "css", "src": "/static/editor.css"}, "editor.js": {"type": "js", "src": "/static/editor.js"} }, "bootloadable": {"Editor": ["editor.css", "editor.js"]}, "jsmods": {"require": [["Editor", "open", [{"__e": "post"}]]]} } The script has to make the module available when it runs, e.g. a chunk of the bundle that calls registerModules() from bigpipe-util/dist/ModuleRegistry. With Vite, give every bootloadable module a small entry of its own and mark its chunk as a module script (see resource map); it shares the chunks of the page, such as bigpipe-util itself, with the entrypoint: resources/js/bootload/Editor.js import { registerModules } from 'bigpipe-util/dist/ModuleRegistry'; import Editor from '../Editor'; registerModules({ Editor }); The other module calls of the response do not wait for it. A call also waits for the bootloadable modules it gets as arguments ({"__m": "Editor"}) and for the class of an instance it calls or gets as an argument. requireLazy(modules, callback) does the same in JavaScript: it loads the resources of the bootloadable modules and calls back with the modules. Modules that are not bootloadable are required right away. import { requireLazy } from 'bigpipe-util/dist/Bootloader'; button.addEventListener('click', () => { requireLazy(['Editor'], Editor => Editor.open(textarea)); });

ifRequired(name, whenLoaded, whenMissing) calls whenLoaded with the module if it is loaded already, and whenMissing otherwise, without loading anything. It returns what the callback returns. A bootloadable module is loaded once all its resources are, any other module when the module loader finds it. import ifRequired from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/ifRequired'; ifRequired('Editor', Editor => Editor.save(), () => console.log('The editor was never opened.')); requireDeferred(name) is a reference to a module that is loaded later. Pass it around instead of the module, and resolve it when you need it: import requireDeferred from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/requireDeferred'; const editor = requireDeferred('Editor'); editor.preload(); // preloads the resources while the network is idle editor.getModuleIfRequired(); // the module, or undefined while it's not loaded editor.load().then(Editor => {}); // loads the resources, rejects if the module can't be required editor.loadImmediately(Editor => {}); // the same with a callback editor.onReady(Editor => {}).remove(); // calls back once it's loaded, `remove()` stops waiting requireCond(condition, whenTrue, whenFalse) requires the module named by the branch that matches, so a page can pick between two implementations without requiring both: import requireCond from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/requireCond'; const Chart = requireCond(window.matchMedia('(max-width: 600px)').matches, 'SparkLine', 'FullChart'); When the server decides, e.g. by a feature flag of the user, it defines the module as the one it chose, see modules the server chooses: only the resources of that one are loaded.

documents.t: A pagelet waits for its css before it is displayed, and for its js before it runs its onload jsmods. With a resource map it can split its resources further: displayResources: what the pagelet needs to be displayed, e.g. its stylesheet. allResources: everything else, e.g. the stylesheet of a dialog it opens or its scripts. They load when the JS of the pagelets loads, and the pagelet runs its onload jsmods once they are loaded. { "id": "feed", "displayResources": ["feed.css"], "allResources": ["dialog.css", "feed.js"], "resource_map": { "feed.css": {"type": "css", "src": "/static/feed.css"}, "dialog.css": {"type": "css", "src": "/static/dialog.css"}, "feed.js": {"type": "js", "src": "/static/feed.js"} } } A stylesheet in allResources does not delay the display of the pagelet.

A bootloadable module with a priority above 0 is preloaded with <link rel="preload"> while the network is idle, higher priorities first, so that it loads fast when the server or requireLazy() calls it. Its scripts run once the browser is idle. { "bootloadable": { "Dialog": {"resources": ["dialog.css", "dialog.js"], "priority": 2}, "Editor": ["editor.css", "editor.js"] } } Bootloader.preloadModules(['Dialog']) preloads the resources of modules right away, e.g. when the user hovers the button that opens the dialog. A pagelet can also prefetch what the user is likely to need next: its prefetchRsrcs load as soon as it arrives, and its prefetchJsmods run once they are loaded. { "id": "feed", "prefetchRsrcs": ["composer.js"], "prefetchJsmods": {"require": [["Composer", "warmUp"]]} }

Dialog shows modal dialogs with the built-in Modal, which has no dependencies. Its markup and classes are those of Bootstrap modals by default, and can be replaced for Tailwind or your own CSS, see Styling. Dialogs can be stacked: each new one is shown above the previous one, and above a ModalLayer shown before it, and Esc closes only the topmost. The server usually opens dialogs with DialogResponse, see Dialogs API. You can also open them from JavaScript.

Builds the dialog from a title, body and footer: import Dialog from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Dialog'; new Dialog().showFromModel({ title: 'Dialog title', body: 'html content', footer: '', controller: 'ModalLogger', backdrop: 'static', });

Shows a dialog from your own markup, the content of .modal: new Dialog().render({ content: `

Option Default Description controller A module name or a function called with the dialog, see below. backdrop true false for no backdrop, 'static' for one that doesn't close it. keyboard true Close the dialog with Esc. animate false Animate showing and hiding. transition 0 Duration of the dialog transition in ms. backdropTransition 0 Duration of the backdrop transition in ms. timeout Show the dialog after this many ms. The method then returns a Promise. label showFromModel only: the aria-label of a dialog without a title. A title labels the dialog itself. autoFocus true Move the focus into the dialog when it is shown, see Layer behaviors. trapFocus true Keep Tab inside of the dialog. refocus true Give the focus back to the element that opened the dialog when it closes. causalElement The element to give the focus back to. The focused element when the dialog is shown by default. hideOnTransition true Close the dialog before a page transition. hideOnSuccess false Close the dialog when a request sent from inside of it succeeds: true for any, or a selector for the elements that sent it. position false Set the top margin of the dialog: true, or { top, centered, ignoreTopInShortViewport }.

A controller is called with the modal and the arguments passed to the method. Use it to react to the events of the dialog: show, shown, hide, hidden and dismiss, which gets the modal, the DOM event and the data-close element that closed it (null for the backdrop and Esc). on(), once() and off() add and remove listeners. ModalLogger.js export default class ModalLogger { constructor(modal, ...args) { modal.on('shown', () => console.log('shown', args)); modal.on('hidden', () => console.log('hidden')); } }

Every dialog is a Layer too, available as modal.layer. The events of the modal stay as they are, the layer adds its own and the behaviors above: new Dialog().showFromModel({ title: 'Unsaved changes', body: '<form>...</form>', hideOnSuccess: true, // close it when the form was saved controller: modal => { modal.layer.subscribe('beforehide', () => formIsDirty()); // return false to keep it open } }); hideOnSuccess listens to the success event of requests whose link or form is inside of the dialog. modal.hide(), the close button, a click on the backdrop and Esc all go through layer.hide(), so beforehide can keep the dialog open for all of them.

The modal brings no CSS. It only sets display (block only when your CSS hides it, so a flex or grid container stays as it is), the z-index of the stacking, and locks the scrolling of the page with inline styles. Everything else is classes, which your CSS styles: Part Default markup container <div class="modal" tabindex="-1"> dialog <div class="modal-dialog"> content <div class="modal-content"> header <div class="modal-header"> title <h4 class="modal-title"> headerClose <button type="button" class="close" data-close> body <div class="modal-body"> footer <div class="modal-footer"> backdrop <div class="modal-backdrop"> While hidden the container and the backdrop have fade, while shown also show, and the body has modal-open while a dialog is open. A click outside of content (or the backdrop) closes the dialog, as does any element with data-close inside of it: <button type="button" data-close>Cancel</button> data-dismiss="modal" of older markup still works.

With animate, the dialog waits transition ms (the backdrop backdropTransition ms) for your CSS transition before it emits shown and hidden.

render() puts your markup into the container template. It finds the parts of it by Modal.selectors, so your markup can use other classes too: Modal.selectors = { content: '[data-modal-content]', // a click outside of it closes the dialog body: '[data-modal-body]', // the dialog moves the focus into it title: '[data-modal-title]' // labels the dialog }; The layer only adds behaviour: it does not add classes, and sets the top margin of the dialog only when you ask for position.

The helpers that the DOM operations are built on. Use them to change the page from your own modules the same way the server does.

import DOM from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/DOM'; const list = document.querySelector('ul.logs'); DOM.appendContent(list, '

    • '); Method Description setContent(node, html) Replaces the content of the node. appendContent(node, html) Inserts HTML as the last child. prependContent(node, html) Inserts HTML as the first child. insertAfter(node, html) Inserts HTML after the node. insertBefore(node, html) Inserts HTML before the node. replace(node, html) Replaces the node with HTML. morph(node, html) Updates the node to match the HTML, keeping the elements that stay. morphContent(node, html) Like morph(), for the children of the node only. remove(node) Removes the node. empty(node) Removes all children of the node. caution The HTML is inserted as is. Escape any user input on the server.

replace() and setContent() throw the old elements away, so focus, typed text, scroll positions and the state of your modules are lost. morph() and morphContent() change only what differs: the elements that stay are the same DOM nodes, with their attributes and text updated. They use the morph algorithm of Alpine and Livewire, adapted from @alpinejs/morph (MIT) and shipped with this package, without a dependency. Elements are matched by their position and tag. Give the items of a list a key attribute or an id to keep them when they are reordered, added or removed. Render the same markup, including whitespace, that the page was rendered with, e.g. the same template. morph() needs HTML with a single root element. Other HTML, e.g. an empty string, replaces the node. A value typed into an input is kept, the value attribute only changes its default. Attributes with @ in their name, like @click, are supported. The Alpine integration of @alpinejs/morph is left out, so the state of Alpine components in the morphed HTML isn't kept.

Find the closest ancestor of a node, including the node itself: import { byTag, byClass, byAttribute, find } from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Parent'; byTag(event.target, 'a'); byClass(event.target, 'card'); byAttribute(event.target, 'data-id'); find(event.target, (node) => node.dataset?.id === '123');
A shortcut for document.getElementById(): import $ from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/$'; $('chart').classList.add('ready');

Form reads the values of a form and locks its controls. It follows what the browser would submit: disabled controls, unchecked checkboxes and radio buttons, and buttons are left out. import Form from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/Form'; Form.serialize(form); // { title: 'Hello', tags: ['a', 'b'], user: { name: 'Jo' } } Form.serialize(form, submitButton); // with the name and value of the button that submitted it Form.createFormData(form, submitButton); Form.hasFiles(form); // whether a file is chosen Form.setDisabled(form, true); // disable every control, and later enable the same ones Form.focusFirst(form); // the first field, else the first button

Fields named a[b] become objects and fields named a[] become arrays, the way PHP reads them, so what you send with AsyncRequest matches $_POST. A repeated plain name keeps its last value, as in PHP. Files are not part of the result: use createFormData() for them. // <input name="tags[]" value="a"> <input name="tags[]" value="b"> <input name="user[name]" value="Jo"> Form.serialize(form); // { tags: ['a', 'b'], user: { name: 'Jo' } }

Form.setDisabled(form, true) disables the controls and remembers which ones were disabled already. false enables only the controls it disabled itself, so a control that was disabled for another reason stays disabled. It accepts any element that holds controls, not only forms. A control that is disabled is not part of what is submitted, so read the values first. The Primer makes the controls of an async form read-only instead while it is saving, which keeps them in the tab order.

FormMonitor tracks whether a form has unsaved changes. While the form is dirty, leaving the page asks the user first: before a page transition with confirm(), and before the page is closed or reloaded with the prompt of the browser, both through Run.onBeforeUnload(). import FormMonitor from 'bigpipe-util/dist/core/FormMonitor'; const monitor = new FormMonitor(document.getElementById('post-form'), { message: 'You have unsaved changes.', // or a function that gets the form, the default warn: true // false only tracks, without asking }); monitor.subscribe('dirty', () => saveButton.disabled = false); monitor.subscribe('clean', () => saveButton.disabled = true); The form is clean when it is created. It becomes dirty when the values of its fields differ from that state (the fields, checkboxes, selects and files that would be submitted), and clean again when they are changed back or the form is reset. Method Description subscribe(event, callback) change (after every edit), dirty and clean (when the state changes). Returns { remove() }. isDirty() Whether the form has unsaved changes. reset() Takes the current values as the saved state, e.g. after saving without a form submit. destroy() Stops monitoring. Done automatically when the pagelet or canvas that holds the form is destroyed, or the page is left.

A form with rel="async" (see the Primer) becomes clean when its request succeeds, see the success event. If the request fails, it stays dirty. A form that is submitted normally becomes clean when it is submitted, so the page that follows is not asked about it. A submit that is cancelled by another handler leaves the form dirty.

The module is created with the form, so the server can start monitoring it: $response->call('bigpipe-util/dist/core/FormMonitor', null, [ \dobron\BigPipe\TransportMarker::element('post-form'), ['message' => 'Leave without saving the post?'], ]);

bigpipe-util is the JavaScript runtime of BigPipe. It sends requests, applies the DOM operations the server responds with and calls the JavaScript modules the server asks for. The server side is usually bigpipe-php, but any backend that speaks the response format works.

A bundler, such as webpack or Vite. bigpipe-util ships both ES modules and CommonJS and doesn't depend on a specific bundler. Loading your own modules by name is up to your application, see step 2. A backend that answers with BigPipe responses, e.g. richarddobron/bigpipe for PHP 8.0+.
npm install bigpipe-util

In your entrypoint (e.g. resources/js/app.js), start the Primer and tell BigPipe how to load your modules. The server refers to them by name, e.g. require('UserLoggedInAlert'), and BigPipe calls the loader to get the module. The loader has to return the module itself (its default export) synchronously. webpack resources/js/app.js import Primer from 'bigpipe-util/dist/Primer'; import { setModuleLoader } from 'bigpipe-util/dist/ModuleRegistry'; Primer(); setModuleLoader(modulePath => require('./' + modulePath).default); Vite resources/js/app.js import Primer from 'bigpipe-util/dist/Primer'; import { setModuleLoader } from 'bigpipe-util/dist/ModuleRegistry'; Primer(); // Eager, because modules are called synchronously. The entrypoint itself is excluded. const modules = import.meta.glob(['./**/*.js', '!./app.js'], { eager: true }); setModuleLoader(modulePath => modules[`./${modulePath}.js`]?.default); Any name is loaded relative to the entrypoint, so require('UserLoggedInAlert') on the server loads resources/js/UserLoggedInAlert.js. Names can contain folders, e.g. Admin/Panel. A loader that returns nothing for a name makes BigPipe throw module "..." was not found. Modules of this package are resolved automatically. The server may refer to them as bigpipe-util/src/... (or bigpipe-util/dist/...); you don't need to handle them in the loader. setModuleLoader() also defines window.require, for code that still uses it; the inline scripts in the next step use a queue instead. Pass { global: false } as the second argument to prevent it. Single modules can be registered under an exact name with registerModules({ Name: module }). They win over the loader.

Defining window.require yourself still works when no loader is set, so existing setups don't have to change. The loader above replaces the bigpipe-util/ branch of the old function: you only write the part for your own modules.

At the end of the page, print the script that sends the pagelets and the modules required during the page render to the browser. With PHP it's one line: layout.php <?= \dobron\BigPipe\BigPipe::render() ?> The entrypoint can be loaded any way: a classic <script src>, async, defer or a <script type="module"> as Vite adds it, before or after this script. The inline scripts queue their calls in window.__bigpipe, and ModuleRegistry runs them in their order once the module loader is set, and every later one right away: (window.__bigpipe = window.__bigpipe || []).push(['arrive', pagelet]); // BigPipe.onPageletArrive() (window.__bigpipe = window.__bigpipe || []).push(['handle', jsmods]); // ServerJS.handle() With an entrypoint loaded before the pagelets, e.g. a classic script in the <head>, every pagelet is displayed as soon as it arrives. A deferred entrypoint displays the pagelets that arrived before it once it runs. Without setModuleLoader(), the queue runs after the entrypoint when the page defines its own window.require, or else once the document is parsed; processQueue() from ModuleRegistry runs it yourself.
